title: What we know about Department for Work and Pensions 'cyber incident'
description: The cause of the "cyber incident" affecting online DWP services remains unclear but Downing Street has not ruled out a cyber attack, with a No 10 spok
body: The cause of the "cyber incident" affecting online DWP services remains unclear but Downing Street has not ruled out a cyber attack, with a No 10 spokeswoman saying: "The investigation is ongoing. I'm not going to get ahead of it."The DWP is working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and the government's Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate the incident and establish the full extent of its impact," she said.She added that there is no evidence that a "malicious actor" is targeting other government departments.Taking services offline is part of a response we have seen in other cyber incidents, as it kicks the hackers out to prevent further intrusion.Cutting internet connectivity can also help responders preserve evidence, which might help if this is indeed some kind of malicious activity.The BBC's cyber correspondent Joe Tidy says the department's actions and wording are reminiscent of the Co-op hack last year.In that incident Co-op said it had taken services offline as a "precaution". Only later was it discovered that it was already too late, as the hackers had successfully breached the firm and stolen the data of 6.5 million customers.And in August, tech firms including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI signed an open letter warning countries and organisations around the world to improve their cyber defences.Today's incident comes just weeks after the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a global programming language.The PHP security flaw prompted a worldwide race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.So far there is no indication that those checks and today's incident are related.

schema.headline: What we know about Department for Work and Pensions 'cyber incident'

title: Most 'swiped-right' man on Tinder charged with rape and assault
description: A man who was once described as "the most swiped-right man on Tinder" is due in court charged with rape following an alleged attack at The Groucho Clu
body: A man who was once described as "the most swiped-right man on Tinder" is due in court charged with rape following an alleged attack at The Groucho Club in central London.Stefan-Pierre Tomlin, 36, who in 2017 was said to be the most coveted man on the dating app, is due at Southwark Crown Court on Monday also charged with two counts of assault by penetration.It follows a Met Police investigation after a woman reported she had been raped inside the private members' club in Soho on 13 November 2024. Tomlin, of Brentwood, was arrested in Hertfordshire on suspicion of rape in 2024 and charges were authorised in September this year. He appeared at Southend Magistrates' Court on 2 November.The Met Police said the woman continued to be supported by specialist officers.Tomlin, who has 454,000 followers on Instagram, describes himself as a pilot, actor and "most right swiped man on Tinder".The Groucho Club was opened in 1985 as a more relaxed alternative to traditional gentlemen's clubs and has a long association with celebrities.The venue was temporarily closed in late 2024 after Westminster City Council suspended its licence following a request from the Met Police but reopened a month later.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Spanish election: Leaders clash in final debate as housing dominates run-in
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing strugglesByNick BeakeEurope
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing strugglesByNick BeakeEurope correspondentReporting fromValenciaSpain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians. The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis."We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.Image caption, Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future."Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says."The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.Image source, Europa Press via Getty ImagesImage caption, Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debateOn housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".Image caption, Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first timeOpponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time."First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says."The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately."We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.Vox called it an "invasion".Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.Image caption, Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist partyIn the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day."The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says."I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.María shakes her head."I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says."People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

schema.headline: Spanish election: Leaders clash in final debate as housing dominates run-in

title: Nathan Lyon: Australia set to drop off-spinner for first New Zealand Test
description: Australia are set to drop off-spinner Nathan Lyon for the first Test against New Zealand, with uncapped Corey Rocchiccioli expected to be named in the
body: Australia are set to drop off-spinner Nathan Lyon for the first Test against New Zealand, with uncapped Corey Rocchiccioli expected to be named in the squad.The omission of Lyon for the Test in Perth from 9-13 December is not thought to be linked to the sandpaper controversy. Lyon was part of the Australia XI in Cape Town in 2018 and, three years later, joined his fellow bowlers in releasing a statement denying involvement in the cheating plot.Lyon has not spoken publicly since the debate over the sandpaper saga re-emerged with the allegation raised in former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering.The decision to omit Lyon, a mainstay of their team for 15 years, is a significant move by Australia and leaves the 39-year-old's international career at a crossroads.With 577 Test wickets, Lyon is sixth on the all-time list, with more wickets than any Australian apart from the legendary Shane Warne. In terms of off-spinners, only Sri Lanka great Muttiah Muralitharan has more.But Lyon has struggled with form and fitness ever since hobbling out of the second Ashes Test at Lord's in 2023 with a calf injury.In the most recent Ashes series of 2025-26, Lyon did not bowl a ball in the first Test in Perth, was left out of the day-night Test in Brisbane, then sustained a series-ending injury in the third Test in Adelaide.Whereas the omission of Lyon would once have been unthinkable, Australia have recently left him out of their XI on a regular basis in order play an extra seamer.Lyon has repeatedly stated his desire to extend his career in order to win Test series away in India and England - challenges Australia face in 2027. He may still be required on the spin-friendly pitches of India, but 29-year-old Rocchiciolli now has the opportunity to be become Australia's number one.Also an off-spinner, Rocchiciolli offers Australia the option of batting depth - he made 140 for Western Australia against Tasmania in the Sheffield Shield earlier this week.Australia host New Zealand for four Tests in December and January.

schema.headline: Nathan Lyon: Australia set to drop off-spinner for first New Zealand Test

title: England in Australia: Jamie Overton claims five as tourists take series lead in Brisbane
description: England outclass Aussies again to take series leadImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, England have won 18 of 21 completed T20s this yearByMatthew
body: England outclass Aussies again to take series leadImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, England have won 18 of 21 completed T20s this yearByMatthew HenryBBC Sport journalistUpdated 1 hour agoThird T20, The Gabba, BrisbaneAustralia 108 (16.5 overs): Overton 5-12, Dawson 3-16England 93-3 (8.5 overs): Cox 33* (14), Donald 32 (13)England won by seven wickets (DLS method)ScorecardEngland reaffirmed their advantage over a struggling Australia in white-ball cricket with a seven-wicket thrashing in the third T20 at The Gabba.Fresh from their eight-wicket win on Tuesday, England bowled Australia out for 108 - the lowest total the hosts have been dismissed for in a T20 at home.Jamie Overton had struggled to this point on the tour but claimed his first international five-wicket haul in taking a remarkable 5-12. Spinner Liam Dawson also chipped in again with 3-16.From there, despite England slipping to 49-3, the most likely route to Australia escaping without defeat appeared to be the weather in Brisbane.After three rain delays, Harry Brook's side reached their revised target of 93 with 7.1 overs to spare, claiming victory via the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method.Opener Aneurin Donald flickered again with a 13-ball 32 while Jordan Cox finished 33 not out as England romped to the finish line on the site of many an Ashes defeat.Having won the 50-over series earlier this month, England can clinch this one with a match to spare by winning the fourth T20 in Sydney on Sunday.Overton's day outEngland's batters, namely Donald and Phil Salt, stole the headlines in Tuesday's win. Here the bowlers, in particular, Overton came to the fore.Overton has had a mixed international career - useful contributions without match-winning performances and often criticised through 51 previous England appearances.His day began with two catches off Dawson in the powerplay as the spinner dismissed Mitchell Marsh in his first over and Sam Harper for 26 in his second to continue England's good run with the new ball. They have taken two or more powerplay wickets in all 11 T20s since the start of the English summer.After that the tall seamer truly got into his work. He found the fast, bouncy Brisbane conditions to his liking and hammered away at a shorter length.The dangerous Jake Fraser-McGurk fell into the trap by sending one from that length to long-on, then Tim David and Nikhil Chaudhary were both hit - David on the arm and Chaudhary flush on the grille - before also being bounced out.Image source, CricVizImage caption, Overton primarily targeted Australia's batters with a hard or bouncer length Joel Davies was another to fall to a bouncer while Ben Dwarshuis was obviously tentative when he nicked behind to give Overton, who also carried on after a nasty blow to the thumb when bowling, his fifth wicket.Brook said afterwards Overton was rewarded for "extra graft" put in during training on Thursday. Overton added: "The last couple of games I've been really disappointed with the way I bowled."Obviously we've not got a few players here who are experienced players so there's the responsibility to step up. "I don't feel I have done that, so it was nice to put in a good performance today."The all-rounder lost his place in England's 50-over side during the series win earlier this month.He may never be a man for all seasons but this was a reminder, with the next T20 World Cup in Australia in 2028 and some bouncy surfaces to be expected in South Africa for next year's 50-over World Cup, of his success when conditions suit.Australia struggling In contrast to England, who have won 18 of 21 completed T20s this year and consolidate their place at the top of the rankings, Australia are struggling badly amid their off-field issues.On the evidence of the previous two matches, the biggest surprise is that they managed to win the series opener in Melbourne.They are without a number of first-team players - most notably Travis Head, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood - but the next generation have shown little to suggest they are ready to step up. For all of Overton's success, this was a supreme batting wicket."A very disappointing night," said captain Mitchell Marsh. "We have to own that. "I said to this young group at the start of the series I don't want them to fear making mistakes."Seamer Riley Meredith offered some fight in a losing cause, bowling in a similar fashion to Overton and dismissing Phil Salt for five and Harry Brook for nine before adding the scalp of Donald.But fielding has also been an issue for Australia. After dropping six catches as a team in Melbourne and putting down Salt early on Tuesday, Chaudhary let a cut from Cox through his hands at backward point when England's wicketkeeper had only one.

schema.headline: England in Australia: Jamie Overton claims five as tourists take series lead in Brisbane

title: 'Poo bags and shovels are part of our Saturday football kit'
description: Image caption, Tucker MacCall has the unenviable job of checking Stow FC for dog dirtByCameron Buttle and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours ago
body: Image caption, Tucker MacCall has the unenviable job of checking Stow FC for dog dirtByCameron Buttle and Andrew PickenBBC ScotlandUpdated 7 hours agoSaturday mornings mean pitch patrol at Stow FC in the Scottish Borders.Before the town's kids can step foot on the pitch, volunteer Tucker MacCall does his rounds with a big black bucket.The "poo bin", with bags, shovel and sand, is now part of the club's Saturday kit."It's getting beyond a joke," he said. "We would normally set up, put the nets up, put the flags out to get the barriers etc ready for the game. Then we have to do a scour of the pitch, to check for dog dirt."The consequences of not doing this dirty job are frustrating. "If we start the game, the game will get stopped, the referee will shout for somebody to bring the poo bin on, remove the dog dirt and then get on with the game again," Tucker said.Image caption, Tucker is one of the Stow FC volunteers who helps clear the pitch for gamesGames have almost had to be abandoned because there was so much poo on the pitch.Tucker said: "If it's found before they land in it, all good and well, but if not, then it's just disgusting and it can cause some serious infection as well."I don't know how people walk on a sports area with dogs and don't pick up. If they did it in the house, they would pick it up and disinfect.  Why do they think it's fine just to leave it there. It's just wrong."Figure caption, People in this Glasgow park said they had witnessed owners not picking up after their dogsThe law in Scotland says that anyone in charge of a dog must immediately pick up and properly dispose of its poo when out and about in public places.Lack of signs is not an excuse.If you are caught, you can face a fine of at least £80.These can be handed out by the police or more usually by council enforcement officers.Stow FC's fight against dog muck is not unique. BBC Scotland News research has found that the problem is getting worse and fewer people are getting caught.We received replies from all 32 councils in Scotland and the data showed the number of complaints about dog fouling had risen by nearly a third in the last five years, from 8819 to 11,742.But during the same time, the number of fixed penalties issued for the offence had dropped from 246 to 164.Edinburgh and Glasgow accounted for most of the complaints - dog walkers in Glasgow were not impressed. See their responses below.The local government organisation Cosla said: "Local government takes the issue of dog fouling seriously, it's important that neighbourhoods are clean."Councils take active steps to address fouling, however there are real challenges facing local authorities - including the standards for evidence requirement as set out within the legislative framework and the difficult financial decisions that councils have faced over the last decade. "Communities also have a vital role in encouraging responsible dog owners to pick up after the dogs and dispose of it responsibly to keep our streets and parks clean."Image caption, Councils hope dog owners act responsibly in their public parksThe difficulties with enforcement are echoed by the leader of Scottish Borders Council, Euan Jardine.He told BBC Scotland News: "It is a complicated process. You do have to catch them in the act, then you have to report it, then you have to take them to court sometimes. "But this is also a matter for the police as well, they can be on top of this. There are ways to do it, people can volunteer,  it can go through community councils."We'll get people to go out with dog poo bags, with green jackets and they say 'Here, I'm friendly, take a dog poo bag'. No confrontations."Unfortunately because of how council budgets are stretched, we can't be on top everything all the time."The approach in the Borders now includes a specialist education officer. Part of their role is to speak to groups about the problems of dog fouling.Rose Hogg was visiting pupils at Tweedbank Primary School and said children were great at passing the message on."They go home, tell their mums, their dads, anybody who listens, which is the aim – the more we can shape them now, in the future it's potentially not going to be as much of a problem," she said."We want to give them that responsibility where they don't even think about it - there's a poo, pick it up, job's done."The children get to practise picking up pretend "squishy poos" and putting them into the bin.Image caption, Education officer Rose Hogg teaches pupils about their responsibilities and they in turn take that home to their parents"We want to make it fun, because fun is memorable," said Rose. "If we get into their heads now, it then becomes normal, it's not a chore – it's just I have a dog, I pick up the poo, it becomes second nature."In the current financial climate it is unlikely there will be increased enforcement. So people like Tucker in Stow can only hope that people get the message and realise the problems they are causing.

schema.headline: 'Poo bags and shovels are part of our Saturday football kit'

title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: How heavyweight rivals changed British boxing forever
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tyson Fury (left) has 36 wins, two defeats and one draw as a professional, while Anthony Joshua has 30 wins a
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tyson Fury (left) has 36 wins, two defeats and one draw as a professional, while Anthony Joshua has 30 wins and four defeatsByKal SajadBBC Sport boxing journalistThey have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.How Fury and Joshua brought big-time heavyweight boxing to BritainBritain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas. Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight."Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard."I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA."The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.Rivals: Fury v JoshuaAvailable nowFigure caption, Will Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua be 'the most defining fight' of their careers?Crossover stars who inspired the next crop of heavyweightsFury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night."You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for £2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".The final question of their legacyYet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place. "Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says. But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved."Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff. But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.Figure caption, Rivals: Fury v Joshua

schema.headline: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: How heavyweight rivals changed British boxing forever

title: Jamal Musiala: What next for Bayern Munich star?
description: Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.During the summer, the public became awar
body: Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life. Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected."He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is said to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.The release clause of £125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.Whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

schema.headline: Jamal Musiala: What next for Bayern Munich star?

title: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal
description: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.Erin Patterson, 5
body: Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.Erin Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday. She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

schema.headline: Erin Patterson: Mushroom murderer launches last-ditch High Court appeal

title: Cold, flu and Covid symptoms: Expert advice and how to avoid the worst
description: Is it a cold, flu or Covid? How to tell the differenceImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 3 hours agoThere are lots of coughs and sneezes doing the roun
body: Is it a cold, flu or Covid? How to tell the differenceImage source, Getty ImagesUpdated 3 hours agoThere are lots of coughs and sneezes doing the rounds at the moment, so how do you know if it might be covid or flu rather than a cold?Here's how to spot the difference and hopefully avoid the worst this winter.What is flu?NHS leaders are already warning that the UK is seeing a "horrible spike" in flu, with hospital cases higher than usual for the time of year.Flu has hit a bit earlier than normal.Vaccines still work against the virus that is constantly changing or mutating. They are updated each year to ensure they are the best match. So far this season, there's a mix of two flu A subtypes, H1N1 and H3N2, circulating in England, says the UKHSA, external.The flu vaccine is designed to protect against all three main types of flu - influenza A(H1N1), A(H3N2) and influenza B. Whichever ends up dominating this winter, or if they all circulate at similar levels throughout, the vaccine should offer broad protection.Some people can get a free NHS flu vaccine, external. Anyone else who wants one can buy it at a pharmacy.Flu symptoms tend to start more suddenly than a cold or Covid, and are usually more severe.Common flu symptoms include a fever, aching muscles and chills.Image source, Getty ImagesIs it a cold? Does cold weather cause it?Cold symptoms tend to be milder and come on more gradually than Covid or flu.It might include a sore throat, as well as coughing and sneezing.Research on the extent to which cold weather impacts our immune systems remains unclear.But darker days mean we typically make a beeline for warm, cosy, indoor spaces.And this environment is perfect for viruses.Schools, nursery and even some workplaces can be like a petri dish with lots of viruses circulating. The Christmas season raises the risks as more people socialise indoors. The same applies to freshers in university halls - where mixing together spreads germs, while heavy drinking and partying further weaken the immune system.Could it be Covid?Image source, Getty ImagesIt is still possible to catch Covid. Common symptoms include a high temperature and a cough, as well as feeling exhausted. One key Covid-specific identifier can be a loss of smell or taste. While no one is told to isolate any more, the advise is try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people if you or your child have symptoms.Most people do not need to take a Covid test if they have symptoms, but they are available to buy in chemists and, while not 100% accurate, they can help confirm or rule out infection.ColdsSymptoms appear graduallyMostly affect nose and throatEarly sign - pressure in your earsChestier, mucus coughFluComes on suddenlyFeel wiped outFever, muscle aches, exhaustionNeed bed restDry coughCovidTypical flu symptomsLoss of taste or smellDiarrhoea or tummy upsetMany of the symptoms between cold, flu and Covid, overlap.But there are some clues that might help you identify the exact culprit.If a cold's coming on, then it often does so gradually. It's going to affect your nose and the back of your throat, while some will get a tickling at the back of the mouth.Another early warning sign can be a build-up of pressure in the ear. If the virus spreads further, it can reach your lungs and cause a pesky cough.Mostly however, these symptoms don't stop us from carrying on as normal.The same can't be said for flu, which typically adds aches, fevers and muscle weakness into the mix. Flu doesn't always mean you have to go to bed, but it might make you feel that way.Since the pandemic, Covid has complicated things further, with similar symptoms to flu.The recommendation is to stay home and rest and recover. However, if you have underlying conditions, experience breathlessness or find symptoms don't ease after three weeks, then you shouldn't hesitate to seek medical advice.Can I help make myself better? Image source, Getty ImagesOur bodies naturally fight viruses and infection, but we can also give it a helping hand with the right medication. Paracetamol: Provided you're okay to take it, this or ibuprofen is the first port of call. Both are really good for helping to bring the fever down and softening any pain that you might have. But remember that lots of cough and cold mixtures include traces of paracetamol, so make sure you're not accidentally taking too muchVitamin C:  This is often thought to help defend against colds. But there's not a huge amount of evidence for this. Unless you're deficient, focusing on a healthy, balanced diet is far more importantVitamin D: A top-up of vitamin D in colder months is recommended by the NHS, because let's face it, we don't usually get much sunlight at this time of year in the UKDecongestant spray: Sure, they feel great and provide instant relief, but using sprays too often can cause rebound congestion- when your nose becomes dependent and swells without a fix. I suggest using them for no more than four of five daysChicken soup: There's little evidence of the dish fighting viruses directly, but its heat can help warm the back of your throat and soothe some of those symptoms. It's also a good way to take on extra fluids, with hydration vital as you battle infection.

schema.headline: Cold, flu and Covid symptoms: Expert advice and how to avoid the worst

title: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough
description: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in deliv
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin."Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English."He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.He said talks were expected to resume in December.On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.The Kremlin appears to be resisting.Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect"."When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin."You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems."It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said."The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.So whose decision was that?"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.He declined to be more specific.But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.They have also plunged much of the city into darkness."[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said."People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

schema.headline: Zelensky tells BBC US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough

title: Fury vs Joshua: Tyson Fury cleared to fight Anthony Joshua after medical checks
description: Tyson Fury has been medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in December after the bout was put in jeopardy by claims of a schizophrenia diagnosis.Fu
body: Tyson Fury has been medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in December after the bout was put in jeopardy by claims of a schizophrenia diagnosis.Fury, 38, spoke of his mental health struggles in a Netflix documentary which was released on Friday, with his wife, Paris, saying he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.But Paris has since retracted that statement, saying he "doesn't have this condition" and Netflix have edited the remarks out of their film.The British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) told BBC Sport: "Tyson Fury has been cleared to box on 11 December."Fury faces Joshua, 37, in a long overdue all-British heavyweight contest at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in the early hours of 12 December.Originally, the Netflix documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion as it sees fit".On Thursday, the BBBoC general secretary Robert Smith told BBC Sport that it was "in the process of dealing with the matter" and that it was "confident he [Tyson Fury] will be absolutely fine".With just two weeks until the British rivals meet for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight world title, Fury has been fully cleared to compete.Fury, who has retired from professional boxing on five occasions, first stepped away from the sport following his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in November 2015.In the Netflix documentary, Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween and had spent two years drinking and taking drugs."I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," Fury said."I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on."I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.Fury is a two-time heavyweight world champion and has lost just two of his 39 professional contests.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: Tyson Fury cleared to fight Anthony Joshua after medical checks

title: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings
description: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home
body: Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day."I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that."So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past. "You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train. Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared. He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face. The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape. "I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others. Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

schema.headline: Huntingdon train attack survivor praises man who saved her during stabbings

title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UK has agreed the deals in a bid to cut red tape for British companiesByPaul SeddonPolitical reporterThe
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The UK has agreed the deals in a bid to cut red tape for British companiesByPaul SeddonPolitical reporterThe UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade. The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days. Fee detailsAccording to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer". 'Extraordinary powers'It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas. The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law"."The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth." schema.headline: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
